query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys reported to date commonly contain both solid solutions and intermetallic compounds. Induction-melted Al- and Mg-rich alloys reached densities of 2.64–2.75 g/cm3 but all had complex structures; Al20Be20Fe10Si15Ti35 combined a density of 3.91 g/cm3 with 911 HV hardness and oxidation resistance at 700 and 900 °C; compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd showed region-dependent compression, plasticity, and corrosion behavior; and reported AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys contained a primary BCC constituent together with intermetallic compounds, with x = 1.0 showing the best property combination in that series. Prior studies have emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, whereas interfacial segregation, interfacial energy, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance remain insufficiently studied. The design must retain a density below 6 g/cm3 and address performance constraints associated with the tendency of Mg and dissimilar constituent elements to form stable intermetallic compounds. Starting from an as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state, what single intervention hypothesis could improve its combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance? State the intervention, its proposed causal mechanism, quantitative or directional predictions relative to the as-processed baseline, the composition and operating or test boundaries, the prior experimental evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with explicit observations that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a specific element, such as Fe, to a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy can improve its combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance by stabilizing the solid solution, suppressing pest oxidation, and forming a stable Cr-rich phase.
generation.material_initial_state: As-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state
generation.intervention: Addition of Fe to the alloy
generation.conditions: Heat treatment and testing at high temperatures (700-900 °C)
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable Cr-rich phase and suppression of pest oxidation
generation.mechanism: Stabilization of the solid solution and formation of a stable Cr-rich phase, leading to improved mechanical and corrosion properties
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance
generation.baseline: As-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy without Fe addition
generation.boundary: Alloy composition, heat treatment conditions, and testing temperatures
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Fe to be added and the optimal heat treatment conditions are uncertain and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys with and without Fe addition, and test their mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with Fe addition does not show improved combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance compared to the alloy without Fe addition, the hypothesis is falsified

Currently, new high temperature alloys are developed based on refractory metals. Nb–silicide-based alloys, also known as Nb in situ silicide composites, have the potential to meet property goals and satisfy environmental and performance targets for future aero-engines [,]. These alloys can have as many as 12 alloying additions, some of which are essential for improving their oxidation resistance and others for improving their strength and creep. These elements include Al (≤5 at %), Cr (≤8 at %), Fe (≤5 at %), Ge (≤5 at %), Hf (≤5 at %), Si (16–22 at %), Sn (≤5 at %) or Ti (10–26 at %) and refractory metals (Mo (≤8 at %), Ta (≤6 at %), W (≤4 at %)). In this work, the RM(Nb)IC alloy Nb–30Ti–10Si–5Cr–5Sn–3Fe–2Al–2Hf (NV2) was studied in the as-cast and heat-treated conditions; its isothermal oxidation at 700, 800 and 900 °C and its room temperature hardness and specific strength were compared with other Sn-containing RM(Nb)ICs—in particular, the alloy Nb–24Ti–18Si–5Cr–5Fe–5Sn (NV5)—and with RCCAs and RHEAs. The addition of Fe (a) stabilised Nbss; A15–Nb3X (X = Al, Si and Sn) and Nb3Si; metastable Nb3Si-m’ and Nb5Si3 silicides; (b) supported the formation of eutectic Nbss + Nb5Si3; (c) suppressed pest oxidation at all three temperatures and (d) stabilised a Cr- and Fe-rich phase instead of a C14–Nb(Cr,Fe)2 Laves phase. Complex concentrated (or compositionally complex) and/or high entropy phases co-existed with “conventional” phases in all conditions and after oxidation at 800 °C. In NV2, the macrosegregation of Si decreased but liquation occurred at T >1200 °C. A solid solution free of Si and rich in Cr and Ti was stable after the heat treatments. In this work, alloy Nb–30Ti–10Si–5Cr–5Sn–3Fe–2Al–2Hf (NV2) was studied in the as-cast and heat-treated conditions: its isothermal oxidation at three pest oxidation temperatures and its room temperature hardness and specific strength were evaluated and compared with other Sn-containing RM(Nb)ICs—in particular, alloy NV5—and with RCCAs and RHEAs. The issues that motivated this research were resolved. The synergy of Fe with Al, Cr, Hf and Sn (a) stabilised Nbss; A15–Nb3X (X = Al, Si and Sn) and Nb3Si, metastable Nb3Si-m’ and Nb5Si3 silicides; (b) supported the formation of Nbss + Nb5Si3 eutectic in the cast microstructure; (c) suppressed pest oxidation in the temperature range 700–900 °C and (d) stabilised a Cr-rich π phase instead of a C14–Nb(Cr,Fe)2 Laves phase. Furthermore, it was shown that complex concentrated (CC) or high entropy (HE) phases coexisted with “conventional” phases in all conditions and after oxidation at 800 °C.
